text:
LISE (to Cyrano, who, passing in front of her counter, has absentmindedly squeezed her hand):
  What is the matter with your hand?

CYRANO:
  Nothing. A sword cut.

RAGUENEAU:
  Did you run into some danger?

CYRANO:
  No danger at all.

LISE (threatening him with her finger):
  I believe you are lying!

CYRANO:
  Would my nose be twitching?
  It would have to be for an enormous lie!
  (Changing his tone):
  I am expecting someone here. Unless it is under the elm,
  You will leave us alone.

RAGUENEAU:
  But I cannot;
  My versifiers will be coming...

LISE (ironically):
  For their first meal.

CYRANO:
  Thou wilt send them away when I give thee the sign...
  The time?

RAGUENEAU:
  Ten past six.

CYRANO (sitting down nervously at Ragueneau’s table and taking some paper):
  A pen?...

RAGUENEAU (offering him the one he has behind his ear):
  A swan’s quill.

A MUSKETEER (magnificently mustachioed, enters and speaks in a stentorian voice):
  Greetings!
  (Lise quickly goes upstage toward him.)

CYRANO (turning around):
  What is that?

RAGUENEAU:
  A friend of my wife’s. A fearsome
  Warrior—so he says!...

CYRANO (taking up the pen again and motioning Ragueneau away):
  Hush!...
  Write—fold it—
  (To himself):
  Give it to her—flee...
  (Throwing down the pen):
  Coward!... But may I die
  If I dare speak to her, say a single word to her...
  (To Ragueneau):
  The time?

RAGUENEAU:
  A quarter past six!...

CYRANO (striking his chest):
  —a single word of all those I have in here!
  Whereas, by writing...
  (He takes up the pen again):
  Very well! Let us write it,
  That love letter I have composed within myself
  And composed again a hundred times, so that it is ready,
  And, placing my soul beside the paper,
  All I have to do is simply copy it out.
  (He writes.—Behind the glass panes of the door, thin, hesitant silhouettes can be seen moving about.)



Scene 2.IV.

Ragueneau, Lise, the musketeer, Cyrano, writing at the small table,
the poets, dressed in black, their stockings sagging, covered in mud.


LISE (entering, to Ragueneau):
  Here are your mud-spattered lot!

FIRST POET (entering, to Ragueneau):
  Fellow craftsman!...

SECOND POET (likewise, shaking his hands):
  Dear fellow craftsman!

THIRD POET:
  Eagle of pastry cooks!
  (He sniffs):
  It smells good in your eyrie,

FOURTH POET:
  O Phoebus of the Roasting Spit!

FIFTH POET:
  Apollo, master cook!...

RAGUENEAU (surrounded, embraced, shaken):
  How quickly one feels at ease with them!...

FIRST POET:
  We were delayed by the crowd gathered
  At the Porte de Nesle!...

SECOND POET:
  Slashed open by sword blows,
  Eight bloodied villains adorned the cobblestones!

CYRANO (raising his head for a moment):
  Eight?... Well, I thought there were seven.
  (He resumes his letter.)

RAGUENEAU (to Cyrano):
  Do you know
  The hero of the fight?

CYRANO (casually):
  I?... No!

LISE (to the musketeer):
  And you?

THE MUSKETEER (twirling his mustache):
  Perhaps!

CYRANO (writing, aside—he can be heard murmuring from time to time):
  I love you...

FIRST POET:
  One man alone, they said, managed to put
  A whole band to flight!...

SECOND POET:
  Oh! It was a curious sight!
  Pikes and clubs littered the ground!...

CYRANO (writing):
  ...your eyes...

THIRD POET:
  Hats were found as far away as the Quai des Orfèvres!

FIRST POET:
  Good heavens! He must have been a savage brute...

CYRANO (doing the same):
  ...your lips...

FIRST POET:
  A fearsome giant, the author of these exploits!

CYRANO (doing the same):
  ...And I faint with fear when I see you.

SECOND POET (snatching a cake):
  What new thing hast thou put into verse, Ragueneau?

CYRANO (doing the same):
  ...he who loves you...
  (He stops just as he is about to sign, and rises, putting his letter into his doublet):
  No need to sign it. I shall give it to her myself.

RAGUENEAU (to the second poet):
  I have put a recipe into verse.

THIRD POET (settling himself beside a tray of cream puffs):
  Let us hear these verses!

FOURTH POET (looking at a brioche he has taken):
  This brioche has put its cap on crooked.
  (He knocks its cap off with one bite.)

FIRST POET:
  This gingerbread follows the famished rhymester
  With its almond-shaped eyes and angelica eyebrows!
  (He snatches the piece of gingerbread.)

SECOND POET:
  We are listening.

THIRD POET (lightly squeezing a cream puff between his fingers):
  This puff is drooling cream. It is laughing.

SECOND POET (biting directly into the large pastry lyre):
  For the first time, the Lyre is feeding me!

RAGUENEAU (who has prepared himself to recite, cleared his throat, adjusted his cap, and struck a pose):
  A recipe in verse...

SECOND POET (to the first, nudging him with his elbow):
  Art thou breakfasting?

FIRST POET (to the second):
  Thou art dining!

RAGUENEAU:
  How to make almond tartlets.
  Beat, until they are frothy,
  Several eggs;
  Into their froth incorporate
  The juice of a choice citron;
  Pour into it
  Good sweet almond milk;
  Put custard pastry
  Along the sides
  Of tartlet molds;
  With a nimble finger, glaze
  The edges with apricot;
  Drop by tiny drop
  Your froth into these wells; then
  Let these wells
  Go into the oven, and, golden,
  Emerging in merry little troops,
  These are the
  Almond tartlets!

THE POETS (their mouths full):
  Exquisite! Delicious!

A POET (choking):
  Homph!
  (They move upstage, eating.)

CYRANO (who has been watching, comes toward Ragueneau):
  Lulled by thy voice,
  Dost thou not see how they are stuffing themselves?

RAGUENEAU (more quietly, with a smile):
  I see it...
  Without looking, for fear it might disturb them;
  And reciting my verses like this gives me double pleasure,
  Since I satisfy a sweet weakness of mine
  While letting those who have not eaten eat!

CYRANO (slapping him on the shoulder):
  Thou—I like thee!...
  (Ragueneau goes to rejoin his friends. Cyrano watches him go, then, somewhat abruptly):
  Ho there, Lise?
  (Lise, in tender conversation with the musketeer, starts and comes downstage toward Cyrano):
  This captain...
  Is he laying siege to you?
